retrieverAlone.section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.3 CNC VERTICAL MACHINING CENTRE: VMC-650
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: CNC Fundamentals
Section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.3 CNC VERTICAL MACHINING CENTRE: VMC-650

**Class and purpose.** The VMC-650 is a CNC machine with a vertical spindle and an automatic tool changer, designed for efficient, accurate production of prismatic parts. The designation suggests an X-axis travel in the region of 650 mm, typical of mid-sized machining centres.

**Construction.** A rigid cast-iron column and base carry the spindle head, which travels in Z, while a saddle and table move in X and Y. Ball screws driven by servo motors, preloaded linear guideways or box ways, and an enclosed working area with doors and interlocks are typical. A belt-driven or direct-drive spindle in the range of 8,000 to 12,000 rpm, with 10 to 20 kW, is common, using a BT/CAT 40 or similar taper. An umbrella or arm-type magazine of about 20 to 30 tools provides automatic tool changes. Flood coolant, chip conveyors, through-spindle coolant and a probing system are common options, and a fourth-axis rotary table is a frequent addition.

**Operating character.** The VMC-650 handles roughing, finishing, drilling, tapping and 3D surfacing in a single setup. Its strength is repeatable accuracy and the ability to run unattended for long periods when combined with proper tool-life management. It demands a good programmer, a trained setter and a disciplined preventive maintenance routine.

**Typical limits.** Part size is bounded by the working envelope and table load. Vertical orientation makes chip evacuation in deep pockets a consideration, which is why coolant and air blast strategies matter.

retrieverAlone.section: SYSTEM FEATURES
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: CNC Programming Handbook, 3rd Edition (excerpt)
Section: SYSTEM FEATURES

CNC unit is nothing more than a sophisticated special purpose computer. The 'special purpose' in this case is a _computer capable of controlling the activities of a machine tool_ , such as lathe or machining center. It means the computer has to be designed by a company that has expertise in this type of special purpose computers. Unlike many business types of computers, each CNC unit is made for a particular customer. The customer is typically a machine manufacturer, _not_ the end user. The manufacturer specifies certain requirements that the control system has to meet, requirements that reflect uniqueness of the machines they build. Basic control does not change, but some customized features may be added (or taken away) for a specific machine. Once a control system is sold to the machine manufacturer, more features are added to the whole system. They relate to the design and capabilities of the machine.

A good example is a CNC unit for two machines that are the same in all respects except one. One machine has a _manual_ tool changer, the other has an _automatic_ tool changer. In order to support the automatic tool changer, the CNC unit must have special features built-in, that are not required for a machine without the tool changer. The more complex a CNC system is, the more expensive it is. Users that do not require all sophisticated features, do not pay a premium for features they do not need.

passages.section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.4 HORIZONTAL BORING MILL: HB-900
passages.text:
Document: CNC Fundamentals
Section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.4 HORIZONTAL BORING MILL: HB-900

**Class and purpose.** The HB-900 is a heavy machine with a horizontal spindle, built for large, heavy parts that need accurate bores, large faces and multiple faces machined in one setup. It serves heavy industry: housings, frames, gearboxes, pump and turbine casings, large valve bodies and machine tool components.

**Construction.** A massive column carries a spindle head that moves vertically. A heavy table or floor plate carries the workpiece, with table travel and rotation provided by a large rotary table. Many designs include a **boring bar or quill** that extends from the spindle, called the W axis, for deep bores, and some add a facing or planer head (a "universal head") for large-diameter faces. Large taper spindles, powerful gearboxes with high torque at low speeds, heavy-duty box ways or hydrostatic guideways, and very large coolant and lubrication systems are characteristic. The designation suggests spindle or travel dimensions in the neighbourhood of 900 mm, typical of medium-heavy boring mills.

**Operating character.** Setting up the workpiece is a major task. The part is lifted by crane, aligned, clamped and checked before cutting begins. The horizontal spindle allows chips to fall away from the cut, aiding evacuation in deep bores. Boring requires attention to bar overhang, rigidity, tool geometry and thermal conditions, since long overhangs deflect and cause taper or chatter in the bore.

**Typical limits.** The HB-900 is slower to set up and costlier than a machining centre, so it is chosen when part size, weight or bore accuracy demand it, not for small parts.

---

Section: HB Series > Heavy-Duty Power & Performance

Accuracy and precision are built into the HB Series at every stage of design and manufacturing. WELE employs finite element analysis (FEA) to optimize casting strength and machine rigidity while minimizing thermal displacement. Cylindrical roller guideways, backlash-free axis systems, and hydrostatic B-axis bearings provide superior positioning accuracy and repeatability. Optional linear scales on the X, Y, and Z axes further boost precision for tight-tolerance machining.

Quality assurance is at the heart of WELE’s production philosophy. Every HB Series machine undergoes strict factory testing under real cutting conditions to verify accuracy, repeatability, and load-handling capability. In addition, automatic tool changers with large tool capacities, right-angle heads, universal milling attachments, and extended quill options allow the HB Series to handle complex part geometries and multi-face machining with ease.

retrieverAlone.section: Horizontal Boring Mill
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: CNC Programming Handbook, 3rd Edition (excerpt)
Section: Horizontal Boring Mill

Horizontal boring mill is just another CNC machine. It closely resembles a CNC horizontal machining center, but it does have its own differences. Generally, a horizontal boring mill is defined by the lack of some common features, such as the _Automatic Tool Changer_ . As the name of the machine suggests, its primary purpose is boring operations, mainly lengthy bores. For that reason, the spindle reach is extended by a specially designed quill. Another common feature is an axis parallel to the Z-axis, called the W-axis. Although this is, in effect, the fifth axis designation (X, Y, Z, B, W), a horizontal boring mill cannot be called a true five axis machine. Both the Z-axis (quill) and the W-axis (table) work in opposite directions - towards each other - so they can be used for large parts and most of _hard-to-reach_ areas. It also means, that during drilling, the machine table moves against an extended quill. Quill is a physical part of the spindle. It is in the spindle where the cutting tool rotates - but the in-and-out motions are done by the table. Think of the alternate method offered on horizon-

tal boring mills - if the quill were to be very long, it would lose its strength and rigidity. The better way was to split the traditional single Z-axis movement into two - the quill extension along Z-axis will move only part of the way towards the table and the table itself - the new W-axis - will move another part of the way towards the spindle. They both meet in the area of the part that could be machined using all other machine tool resources.

Horizontal boring mill may be called a 3-1/2 axis CNC machine, but certainly not a 5-axis CNC machine, even if the number of programmed axes is five. Programming procedures for CNC boring mills are very similar to the horizontal and vertical CNC machining centers.

retrieverAlone.text:

Section: HB Series > Trusted Structural Design & Innovation

The HB Series horizontal boring mills are engineered with a structural design that combines massive rigidity, advanced vibration control, and thermal stability—ensuring the highest levels of performance for heavy-duty and precision machining. At the foundation is a one-piece Meehanite® cast iron base that provides exceptional strength and stability, even under extreme cutting loads. Dual vertical columns and wide-span guideways support the moving components, minimizing deflection while maintaining accuracy across large work envelopes.

To further enhance stability, the HB Series integrates cylindrical roller guideways on the X, Y, and Z axes, which deliver smooth motion, reduced friction, and superior damping characteristics. The B-axis rotary table employs a hydrostatic bearing system, eliminating backlash while supporting workpieces weighing up to 12 tons. This structural approach not only guarantees load-bearing capacity but also provides the precision needed for complex multi-axis machining.

retrieverAlone.section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.3 CNC VERTICAL MACHINING CENTRE: VMC-650
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: CNC Fundamentals
Section: Milling Machines and CNC Technology > 7. Model Profiles > 7.3 CNC VERTICAL MACHINING CENTRE: VMC-650

**Class and purpose.** The VMC-650 is a CNC machine with a vertical spindle and an automatic tool changer, designed for efficient, accurate production of prismatic parts. The designation suggests an X-axis travel in the region of 650 mm, typical of mid-sized machining centres.

**Construction.** A rigid cast-iron column and base carry the spindle head, which travels in Z, while a saddle and table move in X and Y. Ball screws driven by servo motors, preloaded linear guideways or box ways, and an enclosed working area with doors and interlocks are typical. A belt-driven or direct-drive spindle in the range of 8,000 to 12,000 rpm, with 10 to 20 kW, is common, using a BT/CAT 40 or similar taper. An umbrella or arm-type magazine of about 20 to 30 tools provides automatic tool changes. Flood coolant, chip conveyors, through-spindle coolant and a probing system are common options, and a fourth-axis rotary table is a frequent addition.

**Operating character.** The VMC-650 handles roughing, finishing, drilling, tapping and 3D surfacing in a single setup. Its strength is repeatable accuracy and the ability to run unattended for long periods when combined with proper tool-life management. It demands a good programmer, a trained setter and a disciplined preventive maintenance routine.

**Typical limits.** Part size is bounded by the working envelope and table load. Vertical orientation makes chip evacuation in deep pockets a consideration, which is why coolant and air blast strategies matter.

passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.4 Tax examples

### 2.3 Shipping is never taxed

Tax is calculated on the items only. The shipping cost is never taxed, in any country.

The order total is: item subtotal + shipping + tax. Tax is rounded to the nearest cent.

- **Colombia, one air compressor at 289.99 USD delivered in Bogotá:** the items are above 100 USD, so tax is 19% of 289.99 = 55.10 USD. Shipping inside Bogotá is 2.53 USD and is not taxed. Total: 289.99 + 2.53 + 55.10 = 347.62 USD.
- **Mexico, items worth 150.00 USD:** tax is 26% of 150.00 = 39.00 USD. Shipping to Mexico by air is 64.00 USD and is not taxed. Total: 150.00 + 64.00 + 39.00 = 253.00 USD.
- **Any country, one Fishtail End Mill 1mm at 27.50 USD:** the items are below 100 USD, so no tax is charged. The customer pays 27.50 USD plus shipping.
- **Any country, items worth exactly 100.00 USD:** no tax, because tax starts only above 100.00 USD.

The shipping quote in the cart already shows the item subtotal, the tax rate for the chosen country, the tax amount and the estimated total, so customers see the tax before they place the order.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.2 When tax is charged: orders over 100 USD
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.2 When tax is charged: orders over 100 USD

Tax is charged only when the item subtotal of the order is strictly above 100.00 USD.

- An order whose items add up to 100.00 USD or less pays no tax at all.
- An order whose items add up to more than 100.00 USD (for example 100.01 USD) pays tax on the whole item subtotal, not only on the part above 100 USD.
- The item subtotal is the sum of every line in the order: tools, end mills, milling machines and technician services, each at its catalog price times its quantity.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules

This book states the rules Iron & Oak applies to every order: where we deliver, which taxes we charge, how shipping is priced and how long it takes, the six end mills we sell, and how technician service visits are booked and paid. All prices are in US dollars (USD). Iron & Oak ships from its warehouse in Bogotá, Colombia.

These rules are the same on the website, at checkout and when Piper, the Iron & Oak assistant, prepares an order. The prices a customer sees in the cart are a preview: the final amounts are calculated by Iron & Oak when the order is placed, from the catalog price of each item.

Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.2 Fixed air prices

Tools and end mills shipped by air cost a fixed amount per order, whatever the weight:

| Destination | Air shipping price |
|---|---|
| Panama | 36 USD |
| Costa Rica | 48 USD |
| Mexico | 64 USD |
| United States | 86 USD |

Milling machines to these countries are not covered by the fixed price: their freight is quoted by staff.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)

Inside Colombia, shipping is calculated with the domestic road formula:

shipping = 0.215 USD per 100 km of road distance + 0.275 USD per kg + 17.50 USD per cubic metre + 2.50 USD base fee

The road distance is measured from Bogotá to the destination city. Colombia is served to these cities: Bogotá, Medellín, Cali, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Bucaramanga, Cúcuta, Pereira, Manizales, Santa Marta, Ibagué, Pasto, Villavicencio, Neiva, Armenia, Montería, Valledupar, Popayán, Tunja, Sincelejo, Florencia and Yopal. A Colombian city outside this list is refused unless our staff have added a road route for it.

Example: a 2 kg parcel with negligible volume going 400 km by road costs 0.215 × 4 + 0.275 × 2 + 2.50 = 3.91 USD. Orders delivered inside Bogotá (a 16.1 km route from the warehouse) pay about 2.53 USD for a light parcel.

Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 4. The Six End Mills We Sell > 4.4 How end mills are sold

### 4.3 Identifying an end mill from a photo

Customers can send Piper a photo of an end mill. Piper's vision model recognises the six end mills above by their shape and size and tells the customer which one it is, with its price and whether it is in stock, so the customer can reorder the same cutter.

- End mills are sold like other tools: they are added to the cart, priced from the catalog, held for 6 hours while the customer pays, and shipped as part of the tools parcel.
- Tax follows the normal rule: an order of end mills alone pays tax only if its item subtotal is above 100 USD (for example, four 3 mm ball nose end mills at 37.00 USD each = 148.00 USD are taxed).
- **End mills have no warranty.** They are consumable cutting tools that wear with use, so warranty claims cannot be made on them.

### 12.7 Installation and Service Charges

Installation, commissioning, inspection, labor, and travel are charged according to the Service Fee Schedule in Section 23. The inspection fee is USD 180. Labor is USD 95 per hour. Fees are stated on the service quotation before work begins.

Shipping charges are calculated at checkout from the delivery address, the shipping method, and the size and weight of the order. Standard shipping is free for standard-product orders of USD 200 or more before tax. Large-equipment freight is always charged and is not covered by free standard shipping.

2. **Country not served:** a delivery country outside the ten listed in section 1 is refused.
3. **Milling machines:** any order that contains a milling machine has its freight quoted by our staff ("shipping on request"). Machines are large and heavy, so we price each one individually.
4. **Air countries (Panama, Costa Rica, Mexico, United States):** tools ship by air at a fixed price per order.
5. **Road countries (Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia):** shipping is calculated from the road distance from Bogotá, the weight and the volume of the parcel.

All tools, end mills and accessories in one order travel together as a single parcel, with one base fee.

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.6 Delivery times
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.6 Delivery times

The expected delivery time is counted from the day the order is shipped:

- **By road:** 1 handling day + 1 day for every 500 km of road distance (rounded up). For example, a delivery inside Bogotá takes about 2 days, and a 1,200 km road delivery takes about 4 days (1 + 3).
- **By air (Panama, Costa Rica, Mexico, United States):** 1 handling day + 4 days in transit = about 5 days.
- **Distance unknown** (for example machine freight quoted by staff): 1 handling day + 5 days = about 6 days.

These are estimates, not carrier guarantees.

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.4 Road shipping to Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia (international road)
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.4 Road shipping to Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia (international road)

To the South American road countries, shipping uses the international road formula:

shipping = 0.27 USD per 100 km of road distance + 0.25 USD per kg + 15.00 USD per cubic metre + 7.50 USD base fee

The road distance is measured from Bogotá to the destination city. The road distances of the ten largest cities of each road country are already known:

- **Ecuador:** Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca, Santo Domingo, Machala, Manta, Portoviejo, Ambato, Riobamba, Loja.
- **Peru:** Lima, Arequipa, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, Cusco, Huancayo, Chimbote, Tacna, Ica.
- **Brazil:** São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Salvador, Fortaleza, Belo Horizonte, Manaus, Curitiba, Recife, Porto Alegre.
- **Argentina:** Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Rosario, Mendoza, San Miguel de Tucumán, La Plata, Mar del Plata, Salta, Santa Fe, San Juan.
- **Bolivia:** Santa Cruz de la Sierra, El Alto, La Paz, Cochabamba, Oruro, Sucre, Tarija, Potosí, Sacaba, Montero.

Other cities in these five countries can still be served: their road distance is looked up when the order is placed. Until then, the cart shows an estimate based on the straight-line distance, so the final shipping cost can differ slightly from the cart preview.

Example: a 2 kg parcel with negligible volume going 800 km by road costs 0.27 × 8 + 0.25 × 2 + 7.50 = 10.16 USD.

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.5 Milling machines: shipping on request
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.5 Milling machines: shipping on request

When an order contains a milling machine, Iron & Oak staff quote the freight for that order. Until the quote is ready, the order shows "shipping on request" with a shipping cost of 0, and it cannot be paid yet. Once staff enter the freight cost, the customer can pay the order with its order number. Staff quote shipping within the 72-hour hold of the order (see section 3.7).

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)

Inside Colombia, shipping is calculated with the domestic road formula:

shipping = 0.215 USD per 100 km of road distance + 0.275 USD per kg + 17.50 USD per cubic metre + 2.50 USD base fee

The road distance is measured from Bogotá to the destination city. Colombia is served to these cities: Bogotá, Medellín, Cali, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Bucaramanga, Cúcuta, Pereira, Manizales, Santa Marta, Ibagué, Pasto, Villavicencio, Neiva, Armenia, Montería, Valledupar, Popayán, Tunja, Sincelejo, Florencia and Yopal. A Colombian city outside this list is refused unless our staff have added a road route for it.

Example: a 2 kg parcel with negligible volume going 400 km by road costs 0.215 × 4 + 0.275 × 2 + 2.50 = 3.91 USD. Orders delivered inside Bogotá (a 16.1 km route from the warehouse) pay about 2.53 USD for a light parcel.

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.4 Tax examples
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.4 Tax examples

### 2.3 Shipping is never taxed

Tax is calculated on the items only. The shipping cost is never taxed, in any country.

The order total is: item subtotal + shipping + tax. Tax is rounded to the nearest cent.

- **Colombia, one air compressor at 289.99 USD delivered in Bogotá:** the items are above 100 USD, so tax is 19% of 289.99 = 55.10 USD. Shipping inside Bogotá is 2.53 USD and is not taxed. Total: 289.99 + 2.53 + 55.10 = 347.62 USD.
- **Mexico, items worth 150.00 USD:** tax is 26% of 150.00 = 39.00 USD. Shipping to Mexico by air is 64.00 USD and is not taxed. Total: 150.00 + 64.00 + 39.00 = 253.00 USD.
- **Any country, one Fishtail End Mill 1mm at 27.50 USD:** the items are below 100 USD, so no tax is charged. The customer pays 27.50 USD plus shipping.
- **Any country, items worth exactly 100.00 USD:** no tax, because tax starts only above 100.00 USD.

The shipping quote in the cart already shows the item subtotal, the tax rate for the chosen country, the tax amount and the estimated total, so customers see the tax before they place the order.

Section: IRON OAK > 14. Bulk and Wholesale Orders > 14.11 Special-Order Conditions in Bulk Orders

### 14.10 Shipping Arrangements

Bulk orders ship by large-equipment freight or by standard shipping according to the size and weight of the order. The shipping cost and method are stated in the quotation. The customer is responsible for receiving the goods at the delivery address.

Special-order items in a bulk order cannot be cancelled after the supplier order has been placed and cannot be returned for change of mind.

cases.question: How long does a delivery to the United States take?
cases.answer:
Deliveries to the United States are sent by air and typically take about **5 days from the ship date**: 1 handling day plus 4 days in transit. It’s an estimate, not a guaranteed delivery date. In-stock standard orders usually ship within 2 business days after confirmation. 
*Source: Iron Oak Business Rules, “Delivery times.”*

passages.section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.3 Shipping
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.3 Shipping

**How long does shipping take?** Standard shipping takes 3 to 7 business days from the ship date. Express shipping takes 1 to 3 business days from the ship date. In-stock orders ship within 2 business days of order confirmation. Large-equipment freight takes 7 to 15 business days. These are estimates. See Section 16.

**Do you ship heavy equipment?** Yes. Heavy equipment such as air compressors, generators, and welding machines ships as large-equipment freight when the product record says so. The freight carrier arranges the delivery appointment. The customer must be able to move the equipment from the delivery point into the building.

**How are milling machines delivered?** A milling machine is imported, inspected by Technical Services when it arrives, and delivered to the customer's site by large-equipment freight after the final payment. The customer prepares the site as described in Section 16.12. Installation and commissioning by Iron Oak are available as optional services.

**What happens if my welding machine arrives damaged?** Write the damage on the delivery receipt when you receive it, take photos, and report it to Customer Service within 24 hours for freight deliveries, or within 48 hours for parcel deliveries. Iron Oak reviews the case and arranges a replacement, a repair, or a refund, and pays for the return of the damaged item. See Section 16.8.

This policy defines which products can be returned, for how long, and under what conditions. Return windows count in calendar days from the delivery date. A product that is defective is handled under Section 17.12 and the warranty policy in Section 18.

Iron Oak may refuse a return that does not meet these conditions.

New bulk customers pay in full before the order ships. passages.section: IRON OAK > 25. Order Management Policy > 25.14 Exception: Address Error
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 25. Order Management Policy > 25.14 Exception: Address Error

### 25.13 Exception: Cancellation

Cancellation requests are handled under Section 26. A request made before the order is Packed is normally accepted for standard products.

If the address is incomplete or cannot be validated, the order is held in Processing and Customer Service contacts the customer. If the customer does not respond within 5 business days, Iron Oak cancels the order and refunds the payment. If the carrier returns a shipment because of a customer address error, the customer pays the return shipping and the new shipping, and Iron Oak refunds the product price only if the customer asks to cancel.

passages.section: IRON OAK > 26. Order Cancellation Policy > 26.8 Imported Milling Machines: Cancellation Stages
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 26. Order Cancellation Policy > 26.8 Imported Milling Machines: Cancellation Stages

A milling machine order passes through cancellation stages. The stage is decided by the date and time of the cancellation request, compared with the dates recorded in the order file.

- **Stage 1: Before the deposit.** The customer has not paid the deposit. The customer can withdraw at no charge. The quotation simply expires.
- **Stage 2: Early cancellation window.** The deposit has been paid. The request is made within 3 business days after Iron Oak confirmed the deposit, and before Manufacturer Confirmation. The customer receives the deposit back, minus an administration fee of 3 percent of the deposit to cover bank and processing costs. The refund is started within 5 business days.
- **Stage 3: After Manufacturer Confirmation.** The order has been placed with the manufacturer. The deposit is not refundable, because it covers the manufacturer commitment, the production slot, and the import costs that Iron Oak has accepted.
- **Stage 4: After arrival.** The machine has reached the Iron Oak receiving facility. The deposit is not refundable. Iron Oak may resell the machine, and may recover from the customer any documented additional costs beyond the deposit only if the signed quotation states this.

passages.section: IRON OAK > 25. Order Management Policy > 25.12 Exception: Product Unavailable or Backorder
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 25. Order Management Policy > 25.12 Exception: Product Unavailable or Backorder

### 25.11 Exception: Payment Failure

retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Keeping Up with Upkeep > From little to big

knowledge? Do I have the necessary tools?

Do I have the time?

If you have to say no to any one of these questions, you need to think hard before taking on the job. You may be better off hiring a pro.

Which brings us to the big projects, things like replacing the roof, leveling a floor, or pouring a new driveway. Unless you have some really awesome skills, solid experience, and know-how, as well as a workshop full of tools, hiring a pro is best. You may think you know how to build a deck, even if you’ve never done it before. However, there are people who build decks every day, people who know how to do the job right. It’s worth the cost of hiring a contractor to be satisfied with the end product.

Many of the folks who listen to my _Money Pit_ radio show or podcast are homeowners who’ve taken on projects that are way beyond their expertise, require the purchase of expensive tools, and take much longer than expected. And they’re not calling to share how wonderful the projects have gone. They need help putting things back together or advice on how to find someone who can get the monkeys off their backs, so to speak. Don’t get caught in this trap. Be smart. Know your limitations.

I once had a caller to my show ask for help with a plumbing project — after his fifth trip to the hardware store. He figured if he could get a project done in less than five trips, it was worth it before calling a pro! While I don’t share his viewpoint, the key takeaway is that your time has a value, and you can waste a whole lot it if a seemingly simple project gets the best of you!

The chapters in Parts 2 through 5 contain many of the most common small and medium-size maintenance tasks that you can tackle yourself. And when a task really should be left to a pro, I tell you that, too.

retrieverAlone.section: Saving Energy with Insulation > Understanding R-values
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Saving Energy with Insulation > Understanding R-values

years, was the same temperate as the rest of the house! _That’s_ the power of insulation.

**_Oh where, oh where does my energy go? Insulating attics, walls, and floors!_**

When it’s done well, nothing keeps on working — for free — like insulation. In this section, I walk you through all the parts of your home that should be insulated and tell you how to fill in the gaps.

**_WHERE TO START: THE ATTIC_**

If your home just doesn’t seem to stay warm, the attic is the first place you should look. As we all learned in grade school, heat rises. In a house, that means most heat is lost through the ceiling, and most homes simply don’t have enough insulation.

How much insulation do you actually need? Insulation levels vary based on climate. To find out how much you need in your part of the country, open a browser and type **energy star how much insulation do I need?** This will return specific sections of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Energy Star website ( `www.energystar.gov` ), where you can look up the recommendation for your area.

Replenishing sagging or settled insulation or just adding more is a simple DIY project:

1. **Grab a ruler or tape measure and head up to your attic.**

2. **Measure the depth of the insulation you have now and compare that to the recommended amount listed by Energy Star to figure out how much additional insulation you’ll need.**

3. **Most homes have fiberglass insulation, so if that’s what you find in your attic, purchase unfaced fiberglass batt insulation and lay it perpendicular to existing insulation and completely cover the original layer.**

Keep in mind that insulation only works when it’s fluffy. If you plan to use your attic for storage, don’t pile things on top of the insulation. Instead, select a dedicated area for storage near the attic hatch and only use as much insulation there as will fit below the attic floor.

And speaking of the attic hatch, remember that heat rises! Make sure you also add weatherstripping around the hatch and insulate the back of it to prevent energy loss in that area.

**Can Piper identify my tool?** Piper can look at a photo and suggest what kind of product it is and which Iron Oak products are similar. It is a search aid and not a confirmation. If it is not sure, Piper asks you for more information. See Section 34.

**Can Piper assess my machine?** Piper can give a preliminary risk assessment for a milling machine if you provide air temperature, process temperature, spindle speed, torque, and tool wear. The result is Low, Moderate, or Elevated Risk. See Section 35.

**Is Piper's machine assessment a diagnosis?** No. It is a preliminary, advisory assessment based on the data you provide. It does not say which part is failing, it can be wrong in either direction, and it does not replace inspection by a qualified technician.

**Piper says my machine has elevated failure risk. What should I do?** Avoid unnecessary continued operation where appropriate, schedule a professional inspection, and contact Iron Oak Technical Services. Piper can create a Priority service request, which Technical Services schedules within 3 business days for sites in the Standard Service Zone. If you notice smoke, burning smell, sparks, or a loose spindle, stop the machine and disconnect the power.

**Does Piper's prediction mean my machine is definitely failing?** No. A higher risk level means the data resembles conditions linked to failures in the past. Only a technician's inspection can show the actual condition of the machine.

retrieverAlone.section: Microwave Maintenance > ARE APPLIANCE SERVICE CONTRACTS WORTH IT?
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Microwave Maintenance > ARE APPLIANCE SERVICE CONTRACTS WORTH IT?

Appliance service contracts, or extended warranties, are popular additions when you purchase major appliances like refrigerators, dishwashers, and clothes dryers. They offer repair and maintenance coverage beyond the manufacturer’s warranty. Consider the following to determine if extended service contracts make sense for you.

- **Coverage clarity:** Before committing, understand both the manufacturer’s warranty and what the service contract covers. Make sure it includes potential damages and part availability for repairs.

- **Appliance repair reputation:** Assess if the appliance warrants such coverage. Consider its repair frequency and cost compared to replacement. Review my sidebar, “Repair or Replace? How to Decide,” later in the chapter to determine life expectancies of major appliances.

- **Hidden costs:** Be aware of deductibles and additional service fees. Understand the financial implications of each repair or potential contract cancellation.

- **Convenience:** Check if service technicians come to your home or if you need to transport the appliance elsewhere. Consider the continuity of service if you relocate.

- **Provider reputation:** Check review sites to determine the reliability of the company offering the service contract. Avoid contracts from companies with limited history, as recourse may be limited if they go out of business.

So, do extended warranties ever make sense?

Yes, if you understand the terms and assess the risks. In my experience, extended warranties only make sense if you prefer predictable repair costs. However, for most new household appliances, manufacturer warranties often suffice due to low repair incidence.

retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Microwave Maintenance

When it comes to a microwave oven, your job is to keep it clean, use it properly, and call a pro or replace it when it begins to act up.

Here’s why keeping the inside of your microwave clean is so important: Stuck-on food particles eventually turn to carbon and cause arcing, which, in turn, can etch interior surfaces and could even compromise the seal around the door. Always wipe up spills promptly. Keep the interior of the oven and the area surrounding the door clean, using a damp sponge to catch spills and splatters as they occur, or an all-purpose cleaning solution for spills that have been left over long periods of time.

Never use a microwave oven for anything other than what it was designed for — cooking and heating. And only use microwaveapproved containers and dishes.

Given the relatively low cost of microwave ovens and high cost of service repair technicians, it’s usually not worth having a failing microwave oven repaired. Unless the oven is still under the manufacturer’s warranty, my advice is to replace rather than repair it.

   - fixed-price services at their listed price;
   - Emergency Repair at 180 USD per hour for the estimated hours, between 2 and 6 hours;
   - Spindle & Tooling Service at the price set by staff for the job.
3. **The customer pays by order number.** Confirming the booking creates an order with its own order number (IO-...). The customer pays it online with that order number. The normal tax rule applies (tax on visits above 100 USD, 19% in Colombia), and there is no shipping. The payment window lasts up to 72 hours, but never beyond the visit date.
4. **The technician visits.** After the visit, staff mark the booking **Completed**. A booking can only be completed once its order has been paid.

Section: IRON OAK > 7. Milling Machine Maintenance Services > 7.3 On-Site Technical Service

On-site technical service means a technician visits the customer's site to inspect, maintain, or repair a milling machine. The process is the following.

- Service-request process: the customer submits a milling machine service request through Customer Service, Piper, or the online store. Iron Oak confirms the request within 1 business day.
- Customer location: the customer gives the full site address, the contact person at the site, and access instructions. The location decides whether the visit is inside the Standard Service Zone, which is a 150 km radius around an Iron Oak Service Hub.
- Technician scheduling: Technical Services assigns a technician and offers a visit date. The target is to schedule the visit within 5 business days after the customer accepts the quotation, for sites inside the Standard Service Zone.
- Travel considerations: inside the Standard Service Zone the travel fee is USD 60 per visit, and the fee is waived for warranty visits. Outside the Standard Service Zone the fee is USD 60 plus USD 0.90 per kilometer beyond 150 km, each way. Section 23 contains the full service fee rules.
- Inspection procedures: the technician checks the reported symptoms, runs the checks that apply, reviews the maintenance history, and records findings with photographs where useful. The inspection fee is USD 180, and it is credited toward the repair price if the customer approves the repair quotation within 30 calendar days.
- Service quotation: the technician or Technical Services office issues a written quotation for the recommended work.
- Labor charges: labor is charged at USD 95 per hour in 30-minute increments, unless the work is covered by the warranty.
- Replacement parts: parts are quoted separately. Parts are original manufacturer parts or compatible parts as described in Section 22, and the quotation says which kind is used.
- Follow-up report: after the visit, Technical Services sends a written report with the findings, the work done, the parts used, and any further recommendations.

Section: Choosing DIY or Going Pro: Know When to Call for Backup > Getting a quote

If the job in question is really simple — such as a minor furnace service — the price is usually based on an hourly rate with a minimum service call or trip fee. The job isn’t very complicated, and the price is based on a few hours of work. Often, such tasks are so inexpensive that it isn’t worth getting lots of quotes — especially if you know that the company has a good reputation.

Comparing estimates for service work is simpler than tackling extensive rot repair or a roof replacement. For these larger maintenance projects, it’s crucial to define the project’s scope first. Then, ask professionals to provide a quote based on that scope and to estimate the time needed for

completion. This ensures that all quotes cover the same scope of work and use similar-quality materials, allowing for a direct comparison (“apples-to-apples”) between the professionals you’re considering.

passages.section: IRON OAK > 18. Warranty Policy > 18.2 General Warranty Terms
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 18. Warranty Policy > 18.2 General Warranty Terms

### 18.1 Purpose

This policy defines the warranty periods and coverage for products sold by Iron Oak. Warranty approvals are decided only by the Warranty Team. Piper explains the warranty but never approves a claim.

The Iron Oak warranty covers defects in materials and workmanship that appear during normal use within the warranty period. The warranty period starts on the delivery date, except for milling machines, which start on the Commissioning Date. The warranty applies to the original purchaser and requires proof of purchase. When a claim is approved, Iron Oak chooses to repair the product, replace it with the same or an equivalent product, or refund the purchase price when repair and replacement are not practical. The Iron Oak warranty is in addition to the manufacturer's warranty and does not reduce rights under applicable law.

passages.section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.6 Warranty
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.6 Warranty

**How long is the warranty?** Hand tools, power tools, and workshop equipment have a 12-month warranty from the delivery date. Power tool batteries and chargers have 6 months. Safety equipment has 12 months for manufacturing defects. Milling machines have 12 months from the Commissioning Date, never more than 18 months from delivery. Replacement parts and repair workmanship have 90 days. See Section 18.

**How long is the warranty on an air compressor?** An air compressor has a warranty of 12 months from the delivery date. Consumables and wear parts such as filters and hoses are excluded. See Section 18.5.

**How do I file a warranty claim?** Contact Customer Service, use the customer account, or ask Piper. You will need the order number, the product model, the serial number where applicable, the purchase date, a description of the failure, photos or videos, and, for industrial equipment, the maintenance history. The Warranty Team decides the claim. See Section 19.

**What is excluded from warranty coverage?** Exclusions include misuse, abuse, unauthorized modification, improper installation, improper maintenance, normal wear and tear, consumables, accidental damage, operation outside specifications, unauthorized repairs, improper storage, and incorrect voltage or power conditions. See Section 20.

retrieverAlone.section: Benefiting from a Little TLC > YOU GET WHAT YOU PAY FOR
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Benefiting from a Little TLC > YOU GET WHAT YOU PAY FOR

Here’s the first rule of home-maintenance materials: Buy the best that you can afford. Doing so gives your home maximum benefit and protection. If you buy inferior materials, you’ll likely be doing the job over again soon. Worse yet, you may end up spending a hefty sum to make repairs that otherwise wouldn’t be needed had you spent a little more upfront. Not a bad proposition if you enjoy spending all your free time and spare change fixing up your home.

So how do you spell safety when it comes to your home?

M-A-I-N-T-E-N-A-N-C-E!

**_Comfort: You’ll miss it if it’s gone_**

Your house contains a number of systems and components that make it a comfortable place to live. (See Part 2.) Most people take the comfort systems in their house for granted. They don’t think about them until one of the systems breaks down. And then the result is a distinct _lack_ of comfort.

For example, your home’s electrical system powers lights, your refrigerator, your water heater, and your washer and dryer, among other things. You may not think about your electrical system when you turn on lights, grab a cold can of soda from the fridge, take a hot, relaxing shower, or fold your freshly laundered clothes, but if that electrical system breaks down, you’ll quickly realize how much of your day-today comfort depends on it.

Because many of the systems found in houses these days have motors and moving parts, they’re especially vulnerable to wear and tear that, without preventive maintenance, could result in major inconvenience — and, at least at my house, lots of swearing.

retrieverAlone.section: Prolonging the Life of Your Washer and Dryer > REPAIR OR REPLACE? HOW TO DECIDE
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Prolonging the Life of Your Washer and Dryer > REPAIR OR REPLACE? HOW TO DECIDE

As the saying goes, all good things come to an end, and for appliances, that usually means at the least convenient time. When that happens — and it will happen — you need to decide whether it’s worth the expense to repair your broken-down machine or just buy a new appliance and start again.

To make the call, you need to consider the following factors.

- **Type of appliance:** Larger, more costly appliances are usually more costeffective to repair. Lower-cost appliances like disposals or microwaves are rarely worth repairing unless they’re under warranty.

- **Age of the appliance:** The older the appliance, the more likely it is to break down again.

- **Cost of the repair:** Lower-cost repairs make sense for appliances of any age. Spending big on an old appliance is risky.

- **Risk of repetitive repair:** This varies with the age of the appliance, but generally, the older it is, the more likely it is to need ongoing repairs that might exceed the cost of appliance replacement.

A lot to think about? You bet! That’s why some years ago, I developed a chart to provide a handy guideline to compare appliance age, repair cost, and the risk of future breakdowns to determine if you’ll get a return on your investment.

retrieverAlone.section: And Then There Was Rust
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: And Then There Was Rust

#### **IN THIS CHAPTER**

##### **Preventing rust**

##### **Removing rust**

##### **Repairing rust damage**

Rust, the reddish-brown crust that forms on materials that contain iron, is caused by low-temperature oxidation in the presence of water. To maintain metal over very long periods of time, all you have to do is control rust. Fortunately, rust can be removed from metal year after year, layer after layer, without causing appreciable damage to the structural value of the metal. This is the main reason why metal is such a good buy in the long run.

Note that although rust can’t be prevented entirely, you sure can slow it down. In this chapter, I’ll share how to remove rust from metal surfaces and prevent it from coming back.

retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Home Maintenance For Dummies
Section: Saving Energy with Insulation > Understanding R-values

need to buy a _hammer tacker_ — a constructiongrade staple gun that you can find at your local hardware store or home center. If the vapor barrier has become brittle and tears, you can staple or nail directly through the insulation.

- **To replace insulation netting,** wire insulation supports (also called _lightning rods_ due to their speedy installation) are a handy alternative to netting or bailing wire. These lightweight, flexible steel rods hold the insulation in place through spring tension. Just place one end of the rod against the side of a floor joist and bend it slightly so that the other end is forced into place against the face of the opposite joist. (See Figure 6-1.) Use one hand to hold up the insulation and the other hand to whip the lightning rod into place.

**FIGURE 6-1:** Lightning rods are a great alternative to traditional insulation netting, but both do the job.

#### **_Insulating water pipes_**

Insulating accessible water pipes in unheated spaces like crawl spaces and attics (see Figure 6-2) saves energy and prevents pipes from freezing and breaking during very cold weather. It’s also cheap insurance. A burst pipe can spew water for hours or days until it’s discovered. I once was asked to inspect a vacant home just a day before it was scheduled to be sold to a new buyer. When I opened the door to this bi-level, I found the lower level had been converted to a swimming pool thanks to a water pipe that froze and broke days earlier!

Adding pipe insulation is a simple DIY project. Just slip the foam insulation tubes around the pipe and use electrical tape to hold them in place. A serrated knife is a very handy tool for cutting foam insulation to the right length. When you come to a corner, make a 45-degree miter joint so that the insulation covers all sides of the pipe.

Heat tape is a heating appliance that is used to prevent water pipes from freezing during periods of very cold weather, and also to thaw them. If you’ve installed heat tape, don’t insulate over the heat tape. Doing so can cause the tape to overheat and cause a fire. It’s also important to note that heat tape must never be left “on” all the time. It should only be used temporarily.

The warranty period starts on the delivery date, except for milling machines, which start on the Commissioning Date. The warranty applies to the original purchaser and requires proof of purchase. ### 20.4 Cosmetic Damage and Shipping Damage

Cosmetic damage that does not affect function, such as scratches or dents on the housing, is not covered after delivery. Damage caused in shipping must be reported within the periods in Section 16.8 and is not handled as a warranty claim.

In addition to Section 20.3, the milling machine warranty does not cover tooling and cutters; damage caused by a collision or crash of the tool, spindle, or table into the workpiece or fixtures; damage from operating the machine without the required lubrication or coolant; damage caused by unqualified operators working outside the manual; or failures related to the customer's site, such as an unstable floor or poor power quality.

passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.8 Milling Machines

**Can Iron Oak import a milling machine for my workshop?** Yes. Iron Oak imports milling machines on demand by written quotation. The Industrial Equipment Team gathers your requirements, recommends a machine, and issues a quotation valid for 30 days. See Sections 5 and 6.

**How long does a special order take?** The estimated lead time for a milling machine is 12 to 24 weeks from Manufacturer Confirmation. This is an estimate, not a guarantee, and local delivery follows the final payment.

**Can I request a specific configuration?** Yes. A Custom Configuration Order records your options on a Configuration Sheet, which the manufacturer must confirm as available. Once you sign the Configuration Sheet, the order cannot be cancelled except where Iron Oak cannot deliver the confirmed configuration. See Section 26.9.

**Can I cancel a milling machine special order?** It depends on the stage. Before the deposit, there is no charge. Within 3 business days after the deposit and before Manufacturer Confirmation, you receive the deposit back minus a 3 percent administration fee. After Manufacturer Confirmation, the deposit is not refundable. See Section 26.8.

**Do you provide installation?** Yes. Installation and commissioning of a milling machine by Technical Services are optional services included in the quotation. The warranty starts on the Commissioning Date.

**Do you provide milling machine maintenance?** Yes. Iron Oak offers preventive maintenance, corrective maintenance, and on-site technical service. Preventive maintenance is recommended every 6 months or 500 operating hours, whichever comes first. See Section 7.

passages.section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.6 Warranty
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Company Book
Section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.6 Warranty

**How long is the warranty?** Hand tools, power tools, and workshop equipment have a 12-month warranty from the delivery date. Power tool batteries and chargers have 6 months. Safety equipment has 12 months for manufacturing defects. Milling machines have 12 months from the Commissioning Date, never more than 18 months from delivery. Replacement parts and repair workmanship have 90 days. See Section 18.

**How long is the warranty on an air compressor?** An air compressor has a warranty of 12 months from the delivery date. Consumables and wear parts such as filters and hoses are excluded. See Section 18.5.

**How do I file a warranty claim?** Contact Customer Service, use the customer account, or ask Piper. You will need the order number, the product model, the serial number where applicable, the purchase date, a description of the failure, photos or videos, and, for industrial equipment, the maintenance history. The Warranty Team decides the claim. See Section 19.

**What is excluded from warranty coverage?** Exclusions include misuse, abuse, unauthorized modification, improper installation, improper maintenance, normal wear and tear, consumables, accidental damage, operation outside specifications, unauthorized repairs, improper storage, and incorrect voltage or power conditions. See Section 20.

### 18.7 Other Standard Product Categories

Electrical and utility equipment and non-consumable paint and finishing equipment have a warranty of 12 months for manufacturing defects. Building and construction hardware is covered by the manufacturer's warranty where the manufacturer provides one. The product record states any different period.

Milling machines have a warranty of 12 months from the Commissioning Date. The warranty never runs more than 18 months from the delivery date. If the customer commissions the machine without Iron Oak and does not return the signed commissioning checklist, the Commissioning Date is 60 calendar days after delivery.

The milling machine warranty covers manufacturing defects, mechanical defects, and electrical defects in the following components when the machine is used as the manufacturer specifies.

- Gearbox, drive train, and feed mechanisms.

Section: IRON OAK > 32. Data and Customer Information Policy > 32.2 Categories of Information

### 32.1 Purpose

This policy defines what customer information Iron Oak collects, why, who may see it, how long it is kept, and how it is protected. Iron Oak collects only the information it needs to sell products, deliver orders, provide warranty and service, comply with the law, and improve its services.

- Account information: name, email address, telephone number, company details, and credentials.
- Contact and communication records: emails, call records, chat messages, and Piper conversations.
- Shipping and billing information: delivery and invoice addresses, and tax identification for business customers.
- Order information: items, prices, payment status, delivery status, invoices, and returns.
- Payment information: Iron Oak does not store full card numbers. A payment processor handles card data, and Iron Oak keeps only the last four digits, the payment status, and the transaction reference.
- Service request information: requests, quotations, reports, visit records, and photographs.
- Machine information: model, serial number, location, installation and commissioning data, and maintenance history.
- Technical information: telemetry and operating data that a customer shares for a preliminary assessment.

### 18.11 Milling Machines: Maintenance Condition

The customer must maintain the machine according to the manufacturer's manual and the Iron Oak preventive maintenance interval of every 6 months or every 500 operating hours, whichever comes first. For an approved claim on a product that must be sent in for repair, Iron Oak pays the shipping in both directions. cases.question: How is road shipping calculated for deliveries inside Colombia?
cases.answer:
For deliveries within Colombia, road shipping is calculated as:

**$0.215 per 100 km from Bogotá + $0.275 per kg + $17.50 per m³ of parcel volume + $2.50 base fee.**

All tools and accessories in an order travel together as one parcel, so there’s one base fee. The final cost depends on the destination city, parcel weight, and volume. Source: *Iron Oak Business Rules*, section 3.3.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.3 Road shipping inside Colombia (domestic)

Inside Colombia, shipping is calculated with the domestic road formula:

shipping = 0.215 USD per 100 km of road distance + 0.275 USD per kg + 17.50 USD per cubic metre + 2.50 USD base fee

The road distance is measured from Bogotá to the destination city. Colombia is served to these cities: Bogotá, Medellín, Cali, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Bucaramanga, Cúcuta, Pereira, Manizales, Santa Marta, Ibagué, Pasto, Villavicencio, Neiva, Armenia, Montería, Valledupar, Popayán, Tunja, Sincelejo, Florencia and Yopal. A Colombian city outside this list is refused unless our staff have added a road route for it.

Example: a 2 kg parcel with negligible volume going 400 km by road costs 0.215 × 4 + 0.275 × 2 + 2.50 = 3.91 USD. Orders delivered inside Bogotá (a 16.1 km route from the warehouse) pay about 2.53 USD for a light parcel.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 1. Countries We Deliver To
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 1. Countries We Deliver To

Iron & Oak delivers to ten countries: Colombia plus nine international destinations in Latin America and North America.

| Country | ISO code | How we ship tools there |
|---|---|---|
| Colombia | CO | By road (domestic) |
| Ecuador | EC | By road |
| Peru | PE | By road |
| Brazil | BR | By road |
| Argentina | AR | By road |
| Bolivia | BO | By road |
| Panama | PA | By air, fixed price |
| Costa Rica | CR | By air, fixed price |
| Mexico | MX | By air, fixed price |
| United States | US | By air, fixed price |

We do not deliver to any other country. An order with a delivery address outside these ten countries is refused at checkout.

Panama, Costa Rica, Mexico and the United States are served by air because there is no road from Colombia to Central and North America: the Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama has no road crossing. The South American countries are reached by road from Bogotá.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.1 The order in which shipping is decided
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.1 The order in which shipping is decided

Iron & Oak prices shipping with the same rules everywhere (cart, checkout and Piper), applied in this order:

1. **Nothing to ship:** an order with only technician services ships nothing, so shipping is free.
2. **Country not served:** a delivery country outside the ten listed in section 1 is refused.
3. **Milling machines:** any order that contains a milling machine has its freight quoted by our staff ("shipping on request"). Machines are large and heavy, so we price each one individually.
4. **Air countries (Panama, Costa Rica, Mexico, United States):** tools ship by air at a fixed price per order.
5. **Road countries (Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia):** shipping is calculated from the road distance from Bogotá, the weight and the volume of the parcel.

All tools, end mills and accessories in one order travel together as a single parcel, with one base fee.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.6 Delivery times
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.6 Delivery times

The expected delivery time is counted from the day the order is shipped:

- **By road:** 1 handling day + 1 day for every 500 km of road distance (rounded up). For example, a delivery inside Bogotá takes about 2 days, and a 1,200 km road delivery takes about 4 days (1 + 3).
- **By air (Panama, Costa Rica, Mexico, United States):** 1 handling day + 4 days in transit = about 5 days.
- **Distance unknown** (for example machine freight quoted by staff): 1 handling day + 5 days = about 6 days.

These are estimates, not carrier guarantees.

passages.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.4 Road shipping to Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia (international road)
passages.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 3. Shipping Rules > 3.4 Road shipping to Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia (international road)

To the South American road countries, shipping uses the international road formula:

shipping = 0.27 USD per 100 km of road distance + 0.25 USD per kg + 15.00 USD per cubic metre + 7.50 USD base fee

The road distance is measured from Bogotá to the destination city. The road distances of the ten largest cities of each road country are already known:

- **Ecuador:** Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca, Santo Domingo, Machala, Manta, Portoviejo, Ambato, Riobamba, Loja.
- **Peru:** Lima, Arequipa, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, Cusco, Huancayo, Chimbote, Tacna, Ica.
- **Brazil:** São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Salvador, Fortaleza, Belo Horizonte, Manaus, Curitiba, Recife, Porto Alegre.
- **Argentina:** Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Rosario, Mendoza, San Miguel de Tucumán, La Plata, Mar del Plata, Salta, Santa Fe, San Juan.
- **Bolivia:** Santa Cruz de la Sierra, El Alto, La Paz, Cochabamba, Oruro, Sucre, Tarija, Potosí, Sacaba, Montero.

Other cities in these five countries can still be served: their road distance is looked up when the order is placed. Until then, the cart shows an estimate based on the straight-line distance, so the final shipping cost can differ slightly from the cart preview.

Example: a 2 kg parcel with negligible volume going 800 km by road costs 0.27 × 8 + 0.25 × 2 + 7.50 = 10.16 USD.

retrieverAlone.section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.4 Tax examples
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules > 2. Tax Rules > 2.4 Tax examples

### 2.3 Shipping is never taxed

Tax is calculated on the items only. The shipping cost is never taxed, in any country.

The order total is: item subtotal + shipping + tax. Tax is rounded to the nearest cent.

- **Colombia, one air compressor at 289.99 USD delivered in Bogotá:** the items are above 100 USD, so tax is 19% of 289.99 = 55.10 USD. Shipping inside Bogotá is 2.53 USD and is not taxed. Total: 289.99 + 2.53 + 55.10 = 347.62 USD.
- **Mexico, items worth 150.00 USD:** tax is 26% of 150.00 = 39.00 USD. Shipping to Mexico by air is 64.00 USD and is not taxed. Total: 150.00 + 64.00 + 39.00 = 253.00 USD.
- **Any country, one Fishtail End Mill 1mm at 27.50 USD:** the items are below 100 USD, so no tax is charged. The customer pays 27.50 USD plus shipping.
- **Any country, items worth exactly 100.00 USD:** no tax, because tax starts only above 100.00 USD.

The shipping quote in the cart already shows the item subtotal, the tax rate for the chosen country, the tax amount and the estimated total, so customers see the tax before they place the order.

retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Iron Oak Business Rules
Section: Iron & Oak Business Rules

This book states the rules Iron & Oak applies to every order: where we deliver, which taxes we charge, how shipping is priced and how long it takes, the six end mills we sell, and how technician service visits are booked and paid. All prices are in US dollars (USD). Iron & Oak ships from its warehouse in Bogotá, Colombia.

These rules are the same on the website, at checkout and when Piper, the Iron & Oak assistant, prepares an order. The prices a customer sees in the cart are a preview: the final amounts are calculated by Iron & Oak when the order is placed, from the catalog price of each item.

Installation, commissioning, inspection, labor, and travel are charged according to the Service Fee Schedule in Section 23. The inspection fee is USD 180. Labor is USD 95 per hour. Fees are stated on the service quotation before work begins.

Section: IRON OAK > 42. FAQ Knowledge Base > 42.3 Shipping

**How long does shipping take?** Standard shipping takes 3 to 7 business days from the ship date. Express shipping takes 1 to 3 business days from the ship date. In-stock orders ship within 2 business days of order confirmation. Large-equipment freight takes 7 to 15 business days. These are estimates. See Section 16.

**Do you ship heavy equipment?** Yes. Heavy equipment such as air compressors, generators, and welding machines ships as large-equipment freight when the product record says so. The freight carrier arranges the delivery appointment. The customer must be able to move the equipment from the delivery point into the building.

**How are milling machines delivered?** A milling machine is imported, inspected by Technical Services when it arrives, and delivered to the customer's site by large-equipment freight after the final payment. The customer prepares the site as described in Section 16.12. Installation and commissioning by Iron Oak are available as optional services.

**What happens if my welding machine arrives damaged?** Write the damage on the delivery receipt when you receive it, take photos, and report it to Customer Service within 24 hours for freight deliveries, or within 48 hours for parcel deliveries. Iron Oak reviews the case and arranges a replacement, a repair, or a refund, and pays for the return of the damaged item. See Section 16.8.

cases.question: What is the maximum gap allowed between the work rest of a bench grinder and the wheel?
cases.answer:
The work rest must be no more than **⅛ inch (3.2 mm)** from the grinding wheel. Check and readjust it as the wheel wears.  

Source: *SPP 1910.241 Hand and Portable Power Tools*, p. 15.

Install safety guards that cover the spindle end, nut, and flange projections or otherwise ensure adequate operator protection;

- Install adjustable and rigid work rests on offhand grinding machines; and

- Install guards over power belts and drives.

The following are some secondary safeguarding methods, work practices, and complementary equipment that may be used to supplement primary safeguarding or alone or in combination when primary safeguarding methods are not feasible:

- Develop and implement safe work procedures for grinding machine operations.

- Install warning and safety instruction signs.

- Ensure that all operators receive appropriate onthe-job training and supervision until they can work safely on their own.

- Use abrasive discs and wheels that are correctly rated for the grinder’s maximum operating spindle speed. The disc or wheel rating is marked on the disc or wheel in surface feet per minute.

- Inspect and sound test the grinding wheel to ensure that it is not defective, unbalanced, loose, or too small.

- Adjust the work rest to within1 /8 inch of the wheel.

- Do not wear gloves, jewelry, or loose-fitting clothing while operating grinding machines and secure long hair in a net or cap.

- Do not adjust the guard or clean the grinding machine while the abrasive wheel is still rotating.

- Conduct periodic inspections to ensure compliance.

- Perform servicing and maintenance under an energy control program in accordance with the _Control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)_ , 29 CFR 1910.147, standard.

passages.section: HAND AND PORTABLE POWER TOOL SAFETY GUIDELINES > POWERED ABRASIVE WHEEL TOOLS
passages.text:
Document: Hand and Portable Power Tools
Section: HAND AND PORTABLE POWER TOOL SAFETY GUIDELINES > POWERED ABRASIVE WHEEL TOOLS

Powered abrasive grinding, cutting, polishing, and wire buffing wheels create special safety problems because they may throw off flying fragments.

Before an abrasive wheel is mounted, it should be inspected closely and sound- or ring-tested to be sure that it **Powered Abrasive** is free from cracks or defects. To test, wheels should be **Wheel** tapped gently with a light non-metallic instrument. If they sound cracked or dead, they could fly apart in operation and so must not be used. A sound and undamaged wheel will give a clear metallic tone or "ring."

To prevent the wheel from cracking, the user should be sure it fits freely on the spindle. The spindle nut must be tightened enough to hold the wheel in place, without distorting the flange. Follow the manufacturer's recommendations. Care must be taken to assure that the spindle wheel will not exceed the abrasive wheel specifications.

Due to the possibility of a wheel disintegrating (exploding) during start-up, the employee should never stand directly in front of the wheel as it accelerates to full operating speed.

Portable grinding tools need to be equipped with safety guards to protect employees not only from the moving wheel surface, but also from flying fragments in case of breakage.

In addition, when using a powered grinder:

- Always use eye protection.

- Turn off the power when not in use.

- Never clamp a hand-held grinder in a vise.

ABRASIVE WHEEL USE:

- Floor stand and bench mounted abrasive wheels, used for external grinding shall be provided with safety guards (protection hoods).  The maximum regular exposure of the grinding wheel periphery and sides shall be not more than 90 degrees except that, when work requires contact with the wheel below the horizontal plane of the spindle, the angular exposure shall not exceed 125 degrees.

Hand and Power Tool Guidelines    GS-91

Page 15

**Safety guards shall be strong enough to withstand the effect of a bursting wheel.

- Adjusting the work rest, balancing the wheel, cleaning the area around the abrasive wheel and loading and unloading parts or measuring parts while the abrasive wheel is still rotating;

- Attempting to stop a rotating abrasive wheel by hand.

##### **Case History #24**

After grinding a piece of steel on an off-hand grinder, an employee turned off the machine and tried to stop the wheel with a piece of scrap steel. His hand slipped and hit the rotating abrasive wheel, amputating the tip of his left middle finger.

##### **Case History #25**

An employee was operating a large surface grinder to grind a groove into a steel part in a large pump repair shop. The part was secured with a vise and placed on a magnetic table. The employee was trying to measure the groove while the table was moving back and forth beneath the grinding wheel. The safe practice, both written and customary, is to disengage the hydraulics for the table and stop the wheel before reaching in to measure or remove a part. Though experienced at operating this machine and aware of the strict rule, the employee attempted to take measurements while the table and wheel were moving and ground off part of his left index finger.

#### **Safeguarding and Other Controls for Grinding Machines**

You can help prevent employee accidents and injuries by using primary safeguarding methods. Here are some examples:

- Install safety guards that cover the spindle end, nut, and flange projections or otherwise ensure adequate operator protection;

- Install adjustable and rigid work rests on offhand grinding machines; and

- Install guards over power belts and drives.

retrieverAlone.section: Ring Test
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Ontario Hand and Power Tools
Section: Ring Test

# Safety in using a portable grinder

- Always wear eye protection.

- Ring-test abrasive wheels before use.

- Clean material from wheel.

- Let wheel dry before testing.

- Tap wheel with something non-metallic such as the handle of a screwdriver.

- Tap 1/2" from outside edge.

- Rotate wheel 45 degrees and repeat test.

- A sound, undamaged wheel will give off a clear metallic ring. A cracked wheel will give off a dull sound with little or no ring.

- Never exceed the safe grinding in rpm for a stone or disk, which should be specified on the manufacturer’s label. Make sure the maximum rpm of the grinder doesn’t exceed the stone speed. Excessive speed can cause disks and stones to disintegrate with the potential for causing a serious injury.

- Always unplug the tool before making grinder/cutter installations.

- Make sure that the grinding wheel is installed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Use the proper hardware (safety flanges, nuts and blotters) as recommended for holding the wheel in position.

- Make sure that safety guards are in place and properly adjusted before operating.

- If you drop a portable grinder or a wheel, inspect it very carefully for damage.

- Wear hearing protection, especially for extended operation. Wear respiratory protection.

- • Change disk or stone as recommended by manufacturer. Excessively worn disks and stones can shatter in use.

- Grind only on the face or outer circumference of the grinding wheel unless it is specifically designed for side grinding.

- Gloves, aprons, and foot protection may be advisable for some work, especially if hot sparks are being generated.

- Always stand aside when starting a grinder, especially with a newly mounted wheel. Hold it away from you until the tool has run at operating speed before contacting the work. This can prevent injury from a faulty wheel blowing apart.

- Use light pressure when starting the grinding, especially with a cold wheel — too much pressure on a cold wheel may cause failure.

Section: Portable Grinders

Grinding wheels, portable buffers, and wire brushes are a constant source of flying particles and require special caution. The storage, mounting,

and operation of grinding wheels calls for thorough training. Figure 21.54 shows types of portable grinders in common use: straight grinders, with stones half an inch wide or more, by 4 to 8 inches in diameter; and angle, or vertical, grinders with abrasive or sanding disks or cup stones.

retrieverAlone.section: Pencil Grinders and Rotary Files
retrieverAlone.text:
Document: Ontario Hand and Power Tools
Section: Pencil Grinders and Rotary Files

These are normally straight die grinders (some have right-angle drive) which accept compatible cutters (files or burrs) or abrasive grinding points of small diameter, normally under 2 inches. Common types include **pencil grinders** and **rotary files** . These grinders operate at high speeds and must be used with caution. The small-diameter tools run up to about 80,000 rpm and the larger at about 20-30,000 rpm. The files or burrs are sharp and can easily cut you, even when static.

Precautions are similar to those for other grinders, but these tools are often unguarded — an added hazard.

- Use only the accessories recommended by the manufacturer and ensure they are speed-rated at least as high as the no-load RPM on the tool’s nameplate. The wrong accessory, if rotated too fast, may shatter during use.

- Use grinding wheels when working with hard materials. Rotary files are used for soft materials such as aluminum, brass, and copper. Using grinding

wheels on soft materials can cause build-up and excessively load the wheel, with the possibility of wheel disintegration.

- Never over-tighten the collet; it can damage the collet, cutter or wheel. If the tool doesn’t run smoothly, the cutter may be out of balance. Replace it.

- Excessive pressure can bend or break the collet, mandrel, or wheel/cutter. If the grinder runs smoothly without load, but not smoothly under load, too much pressure is being used.

- Maintain a firm grip on all grinding tools. Always keep the tool pointing away from you. Never use a rotary die grinder with the cutter

towards you. A slip could cause serious injury.

- Use a vise or clamp to hold the workpiece securely. Never hold a small workpiece by hand.

Section: Ring Test

- Use light pressure when starting the grinding, especially with a cold wheel — too much pressure on a cold wheel may cause failure.

- Don’t wear loose clothing when grinding.

- Do not use grinders in the vicinity of flammable materials.

cases.question: What is the maximum air pressure allowed when using compressed air to clean?
cases.answer: For cleaning, limit the blow gun to **30 psi (about 207 kPa) or less at the nozzle**. Wear eye protection and use a chip guard; a brush or vacuum is safer for dust and debris. *Source: “Hand and Portable Power Tools,” p. 18.*

passages.text:
Document: Ontario Hand and Power Tools
Section: Air Compressors

Powered by a combustion engine or electric motor, air compressors supply the air for the tool. Keep the manual with the machine and follow its directions. Check the maintenance and setup requirements and stick to a regular maintenance schedule.

There are basic precautions which must be followed for compressors.

- Inspect before use, check hoses and fittings, and never use a damaged unit.

- Keep the belt guard in place.

- When using a gas or diesel powered unit, make sure there is adequate ventilation and avoid inhaling exhaust gases.

- In cold weather, moisture in the air lines can freeze, reducing the efficiency of the equipment and producing potential hazards. Anti-freeze systems are available in addition to the cold weather precaution given below.

**Air hoses** should be kept clear of traffic and not present tripping hazards. A hose that is left on the floor should be

protected against damage by running planks along either side of it. Where possible, suspend hoses over walkways, traffic routes, and work areas, but take care that hoses do not get caught on passing vehicles.

Occasionally workers suffer injuries when compressed air is used to blow dust and dirt from the work area or from clothing. Compressed air can enter the skin and bloodstream with disastrous results. It can also blow particles and dust into the air at high velocity, endangering eyes and lungs. To clean away dust, use a brush or vacuum instead.

Always secure hose connections with wire, safety clips, or chain to prevent whipping, except when automatic couplers are used.

Never kink hose to stop air flow. Turn off the pressure to hoses when the system is not in use.
